tip: Verbs starting with 'be-', 'ver-', 'ont-' skip the 'ge-' in the participle: 'betalen' becomes 'betaald'.
'Terwijl' (while) pushes its verb to the clause end: 'terwijl wij praatten'.
'Om ... te' plus an infinitive means 'in order to': 'om wakker te worden' = to wake up.
'Vinden' is a strong verb: the past changes the vowel to 'vond', plural 'vonden', not a '-de' ending.
'Nieuw' normally becomes 'nieuwe' before a noun: 'de nieuwe manager'. After 'is' or 'zijn' it stays 'nieuw': 'het is nieuw'.
When the subject 'je' follows its verb, the '-t' drops: 'kun je', not 'kunt je'.
Weather uses a dummy 'het' with no real subject: 'regent het vaak' = it often rains.
'Liever' is how you say you would rather: 'wil ik liever thuisblijven' = I'd rather stay home.
'Erbij' is 'er' + 'bij', meaning 'with it': 'een glas kraanwater erbij' = a glass of tap water with it.
An infinitive can work as a noun: 'bewegen' here means moving, the activity itself.
Comparisons of difference use 'dan', not 'als': 'anders dan verwacht' means other than expected.
Dutch glues compounds into one word: 'pepermunt' plus 'thee' becomes 'pepermuntthee'.
Before a noun 'heel' usually becomes 'hele' for 'whole': 'het hele dak' = the entire roof.
In the main clause a separable verb splits, its prefix moving to the end: 'bieden ... aan'.
The '-tje' ending makes a diminutive, always a het-word: 'tuintje' = little garden.
'Pas' before a time means not until: 'pas na middernacht' is not until after midnight.
Strong verbs change their vowel in the participle: 'drinken' becomes 'gedronken'.
'Leeg' normally becomes 'lege' before a noun; the doubled 'ee' shrinks to one 'e' because the syllable opens up.
'Honderden' with '-en' means hundreds, a vague large number; plain 'honderd' would count exactly one hundred.
'Nadenken' here is an infinitive used as a noun: 'na lang nadenken', after long thinking.
'Vlak' before a preposition means right or just: 'vlak voor het examen' is right before the exam.
A double vowel drops to one when the adjective adds '-e': 'groot' becomes 'grote'.
'Het meisje' but 'een klein meisje' – no '-e' because it's a het-word with 'een'.
'Wat een' plus a noun makes an exclamation: 'wat een mazzel' means what luck.
In speech, 'heel' (very) often takes '-e' before another adjective: 'een hele interessante documentaire'.
'Verte' comes from the adjective 'ver' (far) plus '-te', an ending that turns adjectives into nouns.
Asking origin, 'waar' splits from 'vandaan', which lands at the end of the clause: 'waar kom je vandaan?'
'Hoe gaat het' is the set phrase for asking how things are going: 'hoe gaat het op school?'
When 'hiernaast' opens the sentence, the verb 'woont' comes before its subject: 'hiernaast woont een familie'.
'Bij ons thuis' – 'bij' + possessive + 'thuis' means 'at our/their home'.
